utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. This is Wednesday, September 24, 2008, and I would like to welcome our witness, the accused, the counsel for Defence, Mr. Stringer and all his -- and his team, as well as our court reporter and everyone helping us around in the courtroom. We will continue with this cross-examination, but first I need to give the floor to our registrar because he has two IC numbers to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 1D has tendered its objection to documents tendered by the Prosecution through witness Puljic Borislav. This list shall be given Exhibit Number IC 00854. The Prlic Defence team has also tendered its response to the Prosecution's objections to its documents tendered through Witness Borislav Puljic. This response shall be given Exhibit Number IC 00855. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Mr. Scott, welcome, and you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, and all those in and around the courtroom, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Kozulj, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, once again our time is limited and I apologise to you if you were offended in any way yesterday that I had to sometimes intervene to move us along, but as you've come to understand possibly since Monday our time is limited and we have to work quite quickly sometimes. So I hope you'll just understand that, and in fact to pick up on that since we -- where we ended last night and to see perhaps where we need to start today, we were looking at the end of the day at a binder of documents concerning communications with Central Bosnia and Sarajevo, which for the record was P 10633. And based on the testimony and some discussions among counsel toward the end of the day, I want to see where we are at this point. Do I understand correctly that the topic of your testimony on this point, it relates to what we might call -- I was thinking about this and sometimes we call these land-line civilian telephone service, so that's what we primarily we've been talking about. And in looking at the documents in the binder, apart from issues concerning land-line civilian telephone service between Herzegovina and Sarajevo, you do not dispute that there were other means of communication between Herzegovina and Sarajevo from 1992 to 1994; do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I failed to make myself clear yesterday. I would like to say that I'm an expert for civilian communications, and this is what I have been doing for most of my life. Apart from my time at school - and that was a long, long time ago and communications at that time were a completely different thing - I never ever dealt with military communications. So what I've been talking about before this Tribunal had to do with civilian communications used by telecom operators, not only in Bosnia and Herzegovina but throughout the world. Military communications or any other special kind of communications -- well, I don't know enough about that and I cannot testify about that and I cannot be clear about technical details. Surely during the war the situation regarding the civilian telecommunications systems was the way I described them. As far as military communications are concerned, I know really little about that. Naturally, during the war, Mr. Prosecutor, it was possible to communicate it in a variety of ways. It was possible for the international military forces or international humanitarian organizations to secure special telecommunications for some authorities if they wanted to do so because they did have at their disposal the necessary equipment. I know that I sometimes saw military vehicles and vehicles used by various humanitarian international organizations that had radio communications equipment, and they did have in place a network in Bosnia and Herzegovina that they could use for their communications. Now, whether they placed any of that at the disposal of certain persons in Bosnia and Herzegovina who at that time were leading figures in the military or in politics, I don't know that and I cannot say anything about it. If they wanted to do so, they were in a position to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, you just drew my attention on an issue that had escaped me so far. You're talking about communication among international organizations. To your knowledge, all these international organizations, there were many of them on the field, so to your knowledge were they able to communicate among themselves using their own instruments, their own devices? I'm talking, for example, about UNPROFOR. Or did they have to use the PTT lines at one point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, the international forces used their own communications system. I know for a fact that the relay station near Mostar, Planinica, that's its name, there's a radio-TV transmitter there, it was used also to house the radio repeater equipment used by the international forces because they had it under its control, and they even maintained the road leading up to that station. Of course, Mr. President, I don't know what kind of a network it was, what its capacity or capabilities were, and so on, because even if I had been interested in that nobody would have told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just on one point of what you've just said, you remind me about something. The Planinica location which was discussed yesterday, you've just said just now that the international forces during - to use your term - during this time-period were able to install a station there. Generally speaking, Planinica was a location that was under - we could call it - HVO control; correct? I'm not saying the internationals weren't allowed to go there, but generally speaking it was on territory controlled by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Planinica as the relay was under HVO control at all times, and I don't know who made the arrangements, but I know that it was used also by the international armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. All right. Well, thank you for that. Let me go back to my first question and your answer, and -- which was helpful. But let me just focus on a couple of specific items just so we can be as clear as possible. You in particular focused a great deal of your testimony yesterday on the -- the disruption, if you will, of the coaxial cable between Mostar and Sarajevo, and that's what I was focusing on primarily when I was using the terminology what we might call a land-line communication. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And so let me -- in light of that, in light of what you told us just a moment ago, can we just be very clear again then that you do not dispute that apart from such land-line PTT telephone service that there -- you don't dispute that there were other means of communication between Herzegovina and Sarajevo from 1992 to 1994. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, that's not appropriate. Mr. Praljak should be cautioned. That's not appropriate behaviour in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak, please do not interrupt the Prosecutor while he's putting his questions. I don't know what you wanted to say, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a -- unless it's an objection, there is a question pending to the witness and I don't want the witness to be told, with all due respect, influenced by Mr. Praljak's speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Mr. Praljak, you are not supposed to intervene during a question-and-answer session unless you notice that the question has not been put correctly, but you suddenly interrupted the proceedings, we have no idea why. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I do apologise. It's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said it, but now I'm forced to repeat it. Mostar PTT, the Mostar telecom operator, was connected with Sarajevo via a coaxial cable. Mostar had two wireless radio relay stations linking it with Split and Podgorica, and then through those systems and other systems located in Serbia, Montenegro, and Croatia, and so on, it was connected, it had alternative connections with Sarajevo. But the -- there were only three major systems that connected Mostar with the rest of the world, so to speak, and if all three were down then Mostar was cut off from Sarajevo. But please do understand what I'm saying. I'm talking about the telecom operators, telecom operators do not deal with radio stations, unlike the military units; that's just not done, it doesn't exist. Radio units were introduced with mobile telephones, and at that time there was no mobile telephony in our area apart from using analog systems from Croatia which could not reach Sarajevo. This network did not reach Sarajevo. It reached some border areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina, bordering with Dalmatia in Croatia or in Posavina, areas that bordered to the north with Croatia. As far as I know, Sarajevo was too far away for this signal to reach it and for people to be able to receive it and use it. So as far as telecom operators are concerned, and the only telecom operators in existence at that time were public companies, there were no private telecom operators, it was not possible at the time when the telecommunications centre in Mostar was destroyed and when all those lines went down, it was impossible to get in touch both with Sarajevo and with Central Bosnia. Let me say this once again. In order for those lines to be established, first of all you have to have the equipment; second, you have to have the technical solutions, you also have to have personnel, freedom of movement, and the willingness for those communications to be established. So we had excellent personnel, but equipment and freedom of movement, those were the areas where we encountered problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on, please, but on the same topic generally. If you can find your way in the Prosecution binder again, and I believe it is still in the first binder, binder number 1, Exhibit P 04699, P 04699. And while you're doing that, sir, let me say for the record that this is a report on the activities of the HVO HZ HB for the period January to June 1993, so it's an HVO kind of six-month report. And if you find that, please -- for the English speakers I'm particularly interested in page 15, page 15 and I'll see if we can possibly help you. If you find the section in the document -- there are subsections of the document and this one is in a section called: "Military Police Administration," and that's -- I'm just giving you that as a landmark. If you find "Military Police Administration" and then go down several pages until you finally -- you will find a paragraph that starts with: "The situation with wire communications ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if anyone else in the courtroom can assist us in finding the Serbo-Croatian page reference, that will be helpful, in e-court or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, it's a paragraph that starts with the text: "The situation with wire communications ..."

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, could you please direct me to the page that I should be looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I guess it's page 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It appears to be page 20 -- perhaps page 24 of the Serbo-Croatian document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you have that, sir, let me just -- and this is a general HVO report and it says this: "The situation with wire communications is mainly satisfactory. All units, stations, and communication centres are connected to the automatic telephone system as end users of the telephone exchange in Split and local exchanges." I note this in particular because of Judge Trechsel's question yesterday. "Telegraph communications are guaranteed at the level of military police battalion administrations." Now, looking at that information, sir, is that -- do you confirm that information is consistent with what you knew of the status at that time? And again, this is a report for the period January-June 1993.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in line with the situation as it was, it reflects the situation as it was, but we're talking about territories under HVO control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And over on the top of that -- well, in the English carrying over to page 16 and in the following paragraph in your -- in any event in either version I suppose, the following paragraph. I won't again read the same -- whole thing, but I notice at the end of that paragraph it mentions this same location, Planinica, and in general it says this system was "... providing good-quality communications links on 70 per cent of the territory of the HZ HB." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And again, that would be consistent with your knowledge at the time?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If you can then -- all right. I think we'll stop with that for this document for purposes of the time-limits that we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Witness, I note that in this report on page 11 in the English version there's a chapter on the CIS, the security and information service. So I have the following question to ask you. The BiH -- I mean, the ABiH, so in Mostar of the units who were under Arif Pasalic's command, I'd like to know whether these units had to go through the exchange, telephone exchange, controlled by the HVO when they wanted to communicate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time prior to the conflict between the Croat and Muslim side, the communications went through the Mostar PTT. They used the same lines that we did and that all the others did, the same communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But after the conflict started, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The lines went down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So which network were they using to communicate among themselves when they were using the telephone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, before the conflict Arif Pasalic was in the western part of the town and communications with the units that were dispersed around the town for the most part in the eastern part of the town were used -- were using PTT cable network. When the conflict broke out, Arif, Arif Pasalic, crossed over to the eastern side and he was able to use the cable installations in the eastern part of the town. A certain number of people who worked in the PTT went together with him, and they assisted in setting this up. I assume that that's what they did because they certainly had the capacity to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have another question, a little question, but it's quite important for me. Maybe you won't really see the point of this question; however, when telephones are tapped, the tapping is done in the PTT exchange, isn't it? I'd like to know whether you have the answer to this, yes or no; if you don't, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only thing I know is that in the former state all cables led to a special room, and there it was possible to tap into all the telephone lines. That's no longer the case, but at any rate it was possible to do that. But you can wire-tap wherever you want to from point A to point B. There are no limitations to that. You can wire-tap in many places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But when you were heading this enterprise, did you -- were you aware of any tapping that would have been done within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know that and I don't think that PTT was used for that directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have a follow-up question to the previous question. You have said, Mr. Kozulj, that Arif Pasalic after the conflict broke out went to East Mostar and from there he could use the cable communications. Now, I wonder whether I understand correctly. You have told us that the two bridges where the coaxial cable passed had been destroyed and the cable had, therefore, been interrupted. Are you now saying that Mr. Pasalic on the east side had the possibility to hook himself on the cable from there to anywhere and use it? Or have I misunderstood this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Coaxial cables are cables that are used for long -- over long distances, and in a town or in an inhabited area you set up a large network using other cables. Mostar, like any other town, offers all kinds of possibilities in this respect, it is full of cables. So although the bridges were down, it was possible to re-connect the cables on the western side of the town and also on the eastern side of the town and to use the cables that were already in place. They could install an exchange and then use the cables. They could also use --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's the answer to my question. Excuse me, Mr. Scott, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, before we leave that document, I was able to find the reference in the B/C/S version to the other portion I did want to briefly mention to you. It's English page 21, and in the Serbo-Croatian it is page 32, and I'm told that in e-court the B/C/S is on page 34. So 21 in the English, 32 in the B/C/S, page 34 in e-court for B/C/S. And I will say for the record, this is in a part of the report that comes under the section titled: "Health Sector." And on that paragraph that I'd like you to look at, sir, it says: "In the recent period -- in the recent period, the Computer Technology and Communications Department set up a communications system throughout the HZ HB wherever such a service existed," listing a number then -- a number of locations starting with Busovaca, Vitez, Konjic, et cetera. At the end of that paragraph the last two sentences are: "All the problems of the medical services and hospitals were discussed through this communication system. All reports containing data on the wounded and killed were filed in the computer of our service." Did you have any knowledge around this time - again, this is a report for the first six months of 1993 - that there was a computer communications network operating in this fashion?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not an expert in that field. These are military communications that were installed wherever it was necessary to secure communication for the requirements of the HVO. This is the system of packet communication in order to protect the information used by -- and they used the military radio communications network. There is nothing in common that they have with the PTT communications. I don't know how that network was built, what its capacity was, where its nodes were or switchboards or -- I really don't know. I'm not trying to avoid anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may just assist, if I may assist the witness and everyone in the courtroom. This document, this part of the document that Mr. Scott quoted, in the Croatian version it does say "package communication." In the English it's translated as "the communications system," and perhaps this is where the misunderstanding arises between the Prosecutor and the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Tomanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can next ask you to look -- you should have another binder, I'm afraid, which is P 10630, which -- I'll wait for the moment. It has -- it's communications related to Gornji Vakuf during the period January 1993. It's a completely separate binder. If you look at the beginning of the binder -- no, the whole binder is 10630. There you go. Sir, this is a compilation of documents. I believe it's -- there are about 72 communications for the period of January 1993, HVO communications related to Gornji Vakuf. My intention is not to go through all the individual documents with you. It's similar to the binder that we looked at yesterday afternoon concerning Central Bosnia and Sarajevo. Sir, if I -- based on this documentation if I was to represent to you that these records indicate at least 72 HVO communications related to Gornji Vakuf during the period the 5th of January, 1993, to the 31st of January, 1993, would you agree that that appears to indicate a pretty good level of communication?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All -- well, the thing is I don't know what sort of communications they were, whether they were packet communications or -- I don't see that from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Gornji Vakuf always was a territory under the control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And by January of 1993 can you confirm that there was -- again, the term I use today, there was land-line telephone communication between the Mostar region and Gornji Vakuf as of January 1993?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not supposed to exist between Mostar and Gornji Vakuf. They could have existed between Gornji Vakuf and Prozor, and then Prozor was linked via radio or some other way with the other territories. Different options were used in order to link up the regions in the territory under the control of the HVO. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Just very briefly, Your Honour, when you look at these documents that are in this binder relating to communications with Gornji Vakuf, just by looking at them, glancing at them, you can see that this is not exclusively about communications with Gornji Vakuf but also with communications about Gornji Vakuf. So then we have documents of a communication at Ljubusko with a location within Mostar but Gornji Vakuf is also referred to. So I guess that the intention of the Prosecutor is to introduce this number of documents as evidence that there was communication with Gornji Vakuf. However, these documents do not show that, not all of them do at least. I don't have the opportunity to look at all of them, but I already see from the chart that some documents refer to internal office-to-office communications in the building in Mostar, for example, or Ljubusko. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] -- it would be a good idea to get this in Croatian also so that we can follow this. I think this is a duty of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's all in both languages in the binder, the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak, does your lawyer have the documents? Don't they have them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with all due respect, we received the binders yesterday from the Prosecutor, as is the habit here in this courtroom, immediately or shortly before the cross began, that is the practice. But there are documents in the binder which have not been translated. So it is a question of how far the Prosecutor will go with these documents. If we're only talking about the binder or the list of documents that have been shown so far, there is no problem; but if we're going to be dealing with documents that have not been translated into B/C/S then we are going to put in an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I don't think that the Prosecutor wants to go into detail or into contents. He just wants to show that there were means of communication. You just need to look at documents 1301, you can see a stamp on it showing that the document was sent through the telegram number 501. I suppose that that's what the Prosecutor wants to show; he doesn't want to go to the contents of the documents. Only ask the witness based on these documents whether the witness can confirm that there were various means of communication, including telegrams, since we can see that this one was received by telegram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, perhaps this is a bit premature, but I think you should in particular establish or at least allege which way of communication was used. One way that we have not yet mentioned here but is used in -- or was until some time ago, at least by our army, are pigeons, and they are not so vulnerable to shelling. But perhaps you will go into this. Some seem Telex, some may be fax, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, to both Mr. President and Judge Trechsel. And let me start by saying that Judge Antonetti, the President, is correct that it was not our intention to go through the content of each of these documents. We're not arguing at this point what a particular report says or doesn't say, except in one aspect which I'll come back to in a moment. So it was not our intention to go through these documents, and of course it would take us more time than we have, to be perfectly transparent, if we were to try to go through all 72 documents. To respond to counsel's observation, the documents -- all the documents in this binder purport to be either one of two things or both, they either are communications with, to or from, at one end or the other, if you will, the communication line with Gornji Vakuf; or they make reference to information coming from Gornji Vakuf. And the Prosecutor -- as to those particular documents, it's that kind of document the Prosecutor would submit that if there are internal reports among the HVO about what's happening in Gornji Vakuf on a day in January 1993, then that information itself was communicated somehow, unless it was being made up, which presumably was not the case. So to answer those questions. Judge Trechsel, I'm afraid that you're absolutely right, the chart would be more helpful if we had indicated in each item the form of communication. Obviously we didn't. Sorry for that. But if we went through each document, again we would see a variety of whether it was by a fax, whether it was -- many of them will be by packet. There are different forms, Your Honour, but I do have to say in all honesty I couldn't possibly go through each one now to put it on, but I understand in the future it would be helpful to have it on the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not clear to me that what is being affirmed is that the HVO units, or let's say territories under the control of the HVO, had communications -- well, we tried with all our might to secure connections for both civilian and military forces in the territories where they were. I don't see what is controversial about that. The other thing is whether they had connections with the others, with the Serb side, with the Muslim side; this is another question altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me be clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really don't want to take up any more time, but I must admit that I'm a little bit confused with this position. My learned friend has explicitly just said that these 72 documents were not -- well, that it was not the intention to go through all 72 of them. If the documents were given to us yesterday or the plan of documents that are going to be used at the cross, we could have for decency's sake been told not to have to go through all these 72 documents. My team this morning invested about four or five hours -- I mean, I didn't keep track of who did what, but four or five hours to go through all of that. So I must object. This seems like a tactic to me. We cannot be given a binder before the cross as the material to be used at the cross, and then to be told during the cross that we did not have the intention in the first place to go through all of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Mr. Kovacic, I discovered only a few minutes ago this binder bearing the number Exhibit 10630, and it took me only a few minutes to realize what the Prosecutor was endeavouring to demonstrate. It didn't take me three hours to understand; I understood in a matter of seconds and I understood that the Prosecutor wanted to use these documents to try and demonstrate that there were various systems of communication that were working with regard to Gornji Vakuf. From what the Prosecutor says, there are 70 documents showing that. He said he was not going to go into each of the 72 documents, so based on that he was going to tell the witness, I have a binder with 72 documents about Gornji Vakuf. These are military-type documents. Since they are sent to operational zones and there are stamps showing that the documents were recorded or sent by radio telegram or Telex, et cetera, and he was going to ask whether the witness could confirm that that was the way it was working at military level. And the witness was to answer, and he answered already in that way, he said that he was specialised in civil matters, not in military matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Let me add, Mr. Kovacic, I'm a bit surprised at this intervention. Yesterday, we had a file thicker than this one, Exhibit 10633, it looks exactly like this. The Prosecutor dealt with it exactly the way he deals with this one, and I find it difficult to understand that this could be misunderstood. I do not think that any blame falls on the Prosecution in this respect. Mr. Scott, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Honours, the problem lies in the fact that we were given one information and that we, using the minimum standards of work required of us, had to go through those documents. Of course we understood what the purpose was, but we cannot foresee how far the Prosecutor will go with each of the examples. We did understand that he was providing examples, but we cannot anticipate how far he will take these examples. So we're automatically trying to find other documents which confirm this, provide some detailed information, explain things, because based on some documents you really cannot see what it's all about -- I mean, you cannot even see what sort of communication is being discussed. I don't want to take any more of your time on this matter, but I still do believe that it is quite unrealistic to provide the other parties in the courtroom, to the Defence and to yourselves, after all, with 72 documents on the table and say, Well, here are the examples. They could have taken out or extracted those two or three examples and use them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I think that Mr. Scott might take four or five examples, I'm not sure. He -- you took the floor before he even started so -- or finished, so maybe that was -- maybe he was planning -- what are you planning to do, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I must -- let me just say this. I mean, I thought that the Prosecution frankly was going out of its way to be as helpful as possible, albeit for the column on the manner of communication which Judge Trechsel's rightly pointed out would be helpful, I would be happy to supplement the charts and provide that information in the future. I could have stood up, I suppose, and put to the witness -- simply made the good-faith representation that the Prosecution had at least 72 documented instances of communications with Gornji Vakuf in January 1993, and as a person who's expert, at least generally in various forms of communication, what that means -- what that says to him about communications. I simply could have done that with that one single piece of paper. I thought it might be more helpful to everyone in the courtroom and to the witness to have not only the table, but, if you will, the supporting material. And so we were trying to be helpful, not unhelpful, in doing it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My original question to you, sir, was -- and I realize you may not be an expert in every aspect of military communications, but you've talked an awful lot about a lot of things since Monday. And let me go back to my original question, sir. Doesn't this indicate to you in general that there were, in fact, fairly extensive communications going on between -- either to or about Gornji Vakuf in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about information that you have information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, if you want to interrupt the witness in his answer, no; but if it's for something else -- what do you want to say? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, regardless of the anger of His Honour Judge Trechsel, what is being said in this court is imprecise. The question says significant communication, important communication, but three times it is repeated that 72 times there was communication with Gornji Vakuf down. This document does not show that. This is not a correct number, so I'm surprised that neither the lawyers or Their Honours are reacting. This documentation shows or it enumerates the communications in Mostar, Mostar and Ljubusko, and then the elementary preciseness of each engineer is not to use the number 72. How broad something is -- and if we're talking about numbers, we need to quote the number, is it 13? Is it 500? But 72 is used three times after Ms. Kuzmanovic [as interpreted] said that it's not 72. And if you're insisting on preciseness or precision, let's stick to it then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak -- well, my colleague doesn't want you to comment; I'm not of his view. So there is some disagreement or total disagreement within the Trial Chamber. As to this figure, the Prosecutor said that there were 72 documents, but of course throughout that period there must have been many more communications with various zones. We see Kordic, Stojic, HVO Main Staff, et cetera, Boban, there must be many more documents and I guess the Prosecutor made a selection using his research engine or software and found 70 documents bearing the name or with the name of Gornji Vakuf. And based on the 72 documents, he's trying to demonstrate that there must have been various ways of communication. Is this your purpose? So there's not just 72 documents, there are many more, but your services have selected these after doing some research. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I would say it wasn't -- just so the record is clear, it wasn't simply, of course, a matter - and I'm sure the Chamber knows this - it wasn't simply a matter of pushing a particular button on Gornji Vakuf, but also a substantial amount of human -- if you will, human review and confirmation that all of these documents did indicate -- have to do either constituting communications themselves, which -- as will be indicated on the document, or evidencing, being evidence of a fact of communications going on at that time, one or the other, as I indicated earlier. And again, Your Honour, I certainly don't want to debate with the witness the content of any particular document, what was or was not happening on a particular day. But the fact of the communications that were going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, may we just make an observation here. Mr. Scott at page 22, line 13, said: "I realize you may not be an expert in every aspect of military communications, but you've talked an awful lot about a lot of things since Monday ..." Not quite sure where the second half of that sentence gets anybody. We all talk about a lot of things. It doesn't make us an expert on anything. But this witness has said, and I can't claim to be giving the precise words, but this witness has said in the course -- just of today, and he's said it previously in his evidence, first of all, he's had very little dealings with military communications. He's also said something very close, he really doesn't know very much at all about it. So the question still arises: On what basis is all this stuff being put to this witness anyway? Because if the witness does not have the knowledge to speak directly to these matters, then what's being done? And this is objectionable, Your Honour. What's being done is a whole lot of material is being artificially fed through this witness -- no disrespect to the witness, he's just some sort of channel, some sort of conveyer belt, and that's not the right way of doing it -- because if the witness is being asked -- and I'm not absolutely sure, because it's not clear precisely what the Prosecution are doing here and what they intend, but if the Prosecution are saying to him: Do you draw the conclusion from these documents that, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera, given that he doesn't have the expertise, then the witness has no role here at all because those are conclusions which Your Honours should be being invited to draw if the Prosecution say you can draw them, but then that leads us back to a basic point which is: On what basis are the Prosecution permitted to be putting this material before the Court anyway so far as it's not already been admitted into evidence? There are quite a lot of questions there, Your Honour, but they are all pertinent questions and they are all linked. And they're all very much at the heart of the way in which cross-examination should be properly conducted in relation to a witness of this type.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, Mr. Stewart reminds us, but I'd say that already. The witness said on several occasions that he was not competent in military matters. All the documents submitted to him are military documents. He may have some limited competence, I don't know, but this is what Mr. Stewart was pointing out to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I won't go into all the -- I won't respond to all of Mr. Stewart's comments. I think it is -- at least in what we think we're trying to accomplish. Maybe it's -- others think differently, but what we thought we were trying to accomplish, we thought we were going about it properly and in a way that was, as I said earlier, as helpful as possible with the exception of the additional bit of information mentioned by Judge Trechsel. Here's the -- let's go right to the root of this the way this has evolved, and actually this ties together a number of interesting issues. The Prosecution has raised on a number of occasions the importance of the information in the disclosure and the summary provided for this witness. It's all that the Prosecution has to prepare. We're not provided any prior statements in most instances or at all. So let me remind the Chamber, this is the summary, this is the Rule 65 ter summary that we are provided by the Defence for this witness and what it says in the middle of the -- page 21: "He will testify in general about the telecommunications set-up in BiH and how because of the war conditions all," and I emphasize the word all, "communications," without qualification as to type, sort, et cetera, "all communications with Central Bosnia were cut off." Now, that is the evidence -- that is the information the Prosecution was given to prepare to meet the evidence of this witness. Now, if the Prosecution was misled on the scope of this witness's testimony, then, you know, that's -- does -- that does not lie at the feet of the Prosecution. If what we're being told is -- and -- and I must say, not only was it in the summary but on the first day of the testimony the witness himself also made such broad statements. At page 20, 21 of the first day of his testimony when talking about the disruption of communication between Sarajevo and Mostar, the witness said "all communications." It was cut off. There was no way of communicating. Now we're finding as the days go by and as we get to Wednesday, well that's not really so much the case, and that really isn't the scope of this witness's knowledge or expertise. So the Prosecution has prepared on the basis of the information provided to it, including the 65 ter summary, and now it's a little bit like, Well, now the situation has been changed. So, Your Honour, that's -- that's what brings us here and I just wanted to make it very -- this is the reason -- this is one of the reasons why the Prosecution has said since April the importance of receiving fair summaries of what a witness is going to come and say because it says "all communications" with Central Bosnia were cut off and that's what we're preparing -- that's what we're responding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This challenges the Prlic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... too much of your time, but I have to respond to what the Prosecutor has said since we prepared those summaries for them together, Mr. Karnavas and myself. The witness is saying the same thing that he told us at the proofing sessions earlier this year, and that is that all communications with Sarajevo were down when the war broke out. The witness did not recant this. He is still saying that. He has said this ten times today. Likewise, on Tuesday, yesterday, the witness said at least 20 times to the Prosecutor that he had no knowledge of military communications. If that was not sufficient for the Prosecutor to prompt him not to pursue this line of questioning, then I don't know what is enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, I'm very unhappy that we still have to discuss whether a locality is in Central Bosnia or somewhere else, in some other region. I would like to stress that Gornji Vakuf is not in Central Bosnia. We have seen a number of documents indicating quite clearly that Gornji Vakuf is in north-western Herzegovina, in a completely different operational zone. So what the Prlic Defence indicated in their summary for this witness is not corrected by the contents of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it seems that there is a misunderstanding. In the Defence's summary it said all communications, and the Prosecution interpreted this as being all military and civilian communications. This is why he is submitting documents to show that at least military communications were up and running. I think we've all understood the point now. Let's not waste any time on this. Mr. Scott, you might be -- move to something else -- unless Judge Prandler would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I do not want to use too much time on this matter. I believe that it is probably due to the issue that the summaries should be really more carefully drafted and prepared. It was mentioned by the Defence that the summaries are relating only to Central Bosnia, which is true because if I read it I may quote "he," that is, Mr. Kozulj, "will also testify in general about the telecommunications set up in BiH, telecommunications set up in BiH," in this case it is not only Central Bosnia, "and how because of the war conditions all communications with Central Bosnia were cut off." And it continues that "Mostar had been an important communications centre before the war and when Mostar was cut off the whole system collapsed, that is, Montenegro, Croatia, Serbia, Croatia," et cetera. So therefore -- it is end of quotation. So therefore, I believe it is a kind of lesson for every one of us here that the summaries are to be prepared and submitted as -- in a way as broadly and as punctually as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to make it clear -- well, a couple of things. I'm not sure that -- in fairness to the Prosecution and to the Chamber, I'm not sure that the impression that would not have been left with the Chamber on Monday, at the end of the day on Monday, would not have been that the scope of Mr. Kozulj's testimony was in fact a much broader -- and if the testimony had ended on that day, the Chamber might well have been led to believe and might have been -- the Defence might well have been expected to argue in the future, that this witness had, in fact, indicated or confirmed that there was no communication, that all communications had been cut off. With the greatest respect, I submit that that was the impression that the Chamber was left with. Now, I want the record now to be very, very clear as to what the evidence of this witness is and is not, and I think it's clear now that what we're saying is that this witness has only talked about what we might call and can establish that as of June 199 -- May 1992 through April of 1994, is what he's told us, that there were no land-line PTT civilian communications between Mostar and Sarajevo. That is his core position. And beyond that, the witness has told us nothing else about the scope of the communications available and used by the HVO during that period. And the Chamber should understand that and there should be no dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I don't really agree with you. Monday I myself put the question to the witness. I asked him about military communications. It was my own question, because another question had been put and I decided to ask a question on military issues, and the witness -- you can look at the transcript, but the witness -- on Monday, as of Monday already the witness told us that he was not competent when it came to military communications, but I mentioned the issue on Monday. So I couldn't be led -- misled at any moment because I did -- I knew that there were communication -- that communications were both civilian and military so I put the question to him. Of course answered, but he did tell us that there were some elements of regarding military communications that he had no idea about. And then yesterday early in the afternoon I went back at it to talk about wire-tapping and telephone tapping, and there again he limited his answer, saying that he didn't know much about it. So the Trial Chamber could not be misled here. I don't agree with this. And as of now we know that as far as civilian communications is concerned, this witness is well-versed in that; but when it comes to military communications, he's much less competent. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I think we should come to an end with this discussion, and I'm afraid that it has perhaps gone a bit astray. What is the issue? We have a bunch of documents that indicate there was a communication between Gornji Vakuf and other towns, Mostar, or which indicate that there had been such communications. Most of them, it is true, are military and that is not something where technically the witness can say much about. But that, I don't think, is not really so essential. Not all of them are military. If you look at number 13, for instance, or at number 31, these are communications which I think it's difficult to classify as military. Number 13 is a decision of Mr. Prlic and Article -- number 31 is a letter of Mr. Boban to Mr. Izetbegovic. There are others. I think that the document itself speaks for itself to a large extent, that at least marginally I think that the witness is capable to saying that he does not -- he does not see anything here which would invalidate the conclusions the document leads to. So I think the Prosecution could go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel. And again, that brings us -- you're absolutely right, that brings us back to the original purpose and intention of the Prosecution proceeding this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the question that I've put to you several times -- and I'm not asking you to comment on any particular military means, whether a particular communication may have been encrypted, whether a military code might have been used. I'm just simply indicating to you that on the basis of at least 72 documents, and we're talking about a specific period of time, about 20 days in January or 25 days in January 1993 - which the Chamber will understand as a time relevant to the indictment - that there was this extent of communications. And as someone who at least generally knows about communications systems, does that not indicate to you, sir, that there was substantial what we might call real-time communication going on about Gornji Vakuf in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like to be allowed to answer. First of all, Gornji Vakuf, as far as I know, is linked with Herzegovina the way that Madam Defence Counsel explained. It was always linked with the free territory, HVO-controlled territory, in Herzegovina. I don't know the details, but the HVO units had the capability of communicating with each other, either using civilian PTT lines or military lines. But this number, 82, over a certain period, well that's -- wouldn't be too much even if it were over an hour. It's a small number. If we're talking about any kind of communications, a one-page message takes a minute to be transmitted. So we're not talking about a huge volume that would be -- that I would find impressive. That's certainly not impressive from my point of view. It's a very low volume of communications, if that's what you're driving at. Secondly, at the beginning of my testimony I said that all the lines were down and I described the lines that were down. Nobody asked me then: What about military communications? I indicated what lines I meant when I said that lines of communication with Sarajevo were down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, if we can -- in the spirit of all this that we've hopefully clarified in the past 15 or 20 minutes, if I can ask you to next go to Exhibit P 10632, which should be in binder number 2 of the general -- what you might call the general Prosecution -- no, I'm sorry -- it may be separate. It may indeed be separate, my apologies, but it's Exhibit 10632, it's sort of the identical format and type of document as the one we were just looking at. These happen to relate to another -- the courtroom will know an important time-period and an important location, mid-April 1993, I believe Vitez and Ahmici are indeed in Central Bosnia. And by these records, sir, I will explain further in a moment, this document would indicate that there were at least 38 HVO communications related to these locations between the days, the 13th of April and the 25th of April, 1993, and in particular in this instance -- the reason I say there's only -- I think there's only -- I think there's only 12 documents but I say there's 38 communications, if I can direct your attention and the courtroom's attention in particular to item number 4 which is tabbed in that set of materials as 00463 is the third document in the binder -- no, excuse me, it's the fourth overall document in the binder -- well, use the tab numbers. I'm sorry. It may be -- P 00463. Sir, this is a -- these are two pages out of the HVO headquarters communication log. This was the log kept at the HVO headquarters in Mostar. And if you look down the page, on the 16th of April, 1993, you will see the time and a description of the communication. For example, if you look at -- if you look at, for example, at 16th of April, 1993, at 0145 hours, it refers to a cable number 2028 from the Vitez Vitezovi special-purposes unit sent to Bruno Stojic, Milivoj Petkovic, Ivan Primorac. Do you see that as one example?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you see -- if you just scan down the page and the references, in particular the ones that refer to Vitez, for example -- another example, 2032, number 2032, 16 April, 1993, at 0230 hours, cable number 2032, sent by Vitez to Mate Boban, Franjo Tudjman, Bruno Stojic, and Milivoj Petkovic. Now, do you see the nature -- you see the way this log-book is laid out; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And my question to you about this binder, sir, is: Again, does that not indicate to you a significant amount of real-time communication among the HVO about the Vitez-Ahmici area in mid-April 1993?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this document is accurate, then there was some kind of communication. I don't know how it proceeded, what equipment was used. It would appear from this that it was packet radio communication, but I'm not familiar with this protocol, with this type of record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this is a military document, obviously it's extremely accurate, and it's just an excerpt. It would have been maybe useful to have the entire register or log-book. But we note that on April 16, 1993, at 1.00 in the morning, 1.00 a.m., a document is sent. I also note, and I'm sure everyone noted also, that all these messages have a number, an order number. On April 16 the document in the log-book is number 2024, which means probably that from January 1st, 1993, to April 16, 1993, there were probably 2.000 cables sent or 2.000 documents or messages sent and recorded in this log-book. And if we have 2.000 of them, that means that there was quite some communications going on. What can you say about this, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can see from this overview, first of all, that this is packet communications that used a radio system used by the HVO. That's what I think. I can't be certain. And secondly, that this would be a normal flow of information at a normal pace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if we can deal with the final bundle of a similar nature, which is -- again it will be a separate -- I believe it will be a separate binder next to you P 01 -- my apology, P 10631, P 10631, and this is a series of documents about communications related to Vares and Stupni Do during the time-period the 19th through the 27th of October of 1993. And in this particular instance I believe there's documentation here reflecting a total of -- well, there's 56 documents here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have to clarify to the Chamber that there was an error. When the -- if you look at the last a page of the document you'll see that it's been numbered 55 so one would -- one would think that there's 55 items. Unfortunately, if you look back at the first page, the last two items on the first page for whatever reason didn't get numbered. So the real number is 55 plus two, which is 57. And the reason I said "56," is because item 55 is actually out of the time-period I just indicated but was included because it was a report prepared by Ivica Rajic on Stupni Do, specifically in response to one of the earlier communications. So we did add that one document outside the time-period because it was directly responsive to one of the documents that were included. So there were 56 documents related to communications related to Stupni Do during the period 19 to the 27th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you is the same. Does that not indicate to you, once again, a substantial amount of effective or real-time communication in the HVO about events happening in Vares and Stupni Do in the latter part of October 1993?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to object to the form of this question. The Prosecutor mentions events that happened in Vares and Stupni Do. The witness does not have time to read through all those documents and he doesn't have to know about the events that are discussed here, and we have to go back to the same issue, communications. Again, we have 50 or 50-odd military communications and the witness is going to give us the same answer. I don't know where this leads and I don't know why we're wasting our time with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say that I fully support my colleague's objection. It appears to me that this is yet another tactical attempt on the part of the Prosecution to reach -- to get to the topic of Stupni Do through cross-examination regardless of the fact that this was not discussed in direct examination. In other words, to bypass your decision regarding whether in the cross-examination they can or cannot deal with topics that were not dealt in direct during the cross-examination. And the same thing happened a little while ago with Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, I don't think that Mr. Scott intends to deal with this topic of Vares and Stupni Do. We've spent hundreds of hours on it already. I believe that what he intends to do, what he wants to do, is to demonstrate that during this period, from October 19 to 27, there were some -- so much -- so many communications going on, that were exchanged. Am I right, Mr. Scott, is that what you want to demonstrate I assume?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I don't know how I can be more transparent than this. Again, we received a summary from the witness that said no communications with Central Bosnia. I met with my people that I work with and we said what are some of the key events that the Chamber might be interested in, and we can look at the communications around those time-periods and those locations. I'm not going to talk about what happened at Stupni Do on the 23rd and 24th of October, but these are communications on that topic at that time. I thought the Chamber might be interested to know that in the scope of this witness given the representations made about testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you'll allow me just a few sentences. As far as I was able to see, those documents are either fully or for the most part already admitted into evidence as exhibits in this trial, and we've discussed them with witnesses who were either in Vares or in Kiseljak. None of the Defence teams ever contested the claim that the communications that are described in those documents actually occurred, and we had witnesses who explained to us how package radio system works and how some notifications were sent from Kiseljak to Mostar and the other way around, and I really think that it is superfluous to keep asking this witness, who has told us so many times he's not familiar with military communications, about things that we heard in this courtroom -- we heard that it was distributed over military package radio communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, let's not start from scratch again. Please put your question to the witness and go to the heart of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question is the same one that I did put I believe a few moments ago before counsels' interventions. Sir, the question I'm putting to you now is the same question I put to you about the earlier bundles or binders and that is: Does this not indicate, sir, a - what word do I use? - a significant amount, a significant number -- volume of communications among the HVO about a particular location, Stupni Do and Vares, at a particular time-period, the 27th of October -- excuse me, I'm sorry, the 19th -- I lost my note on that -- during this time in October 1993. Does it not indicate that to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection to the imprecision in the question because of the use of the term "significant." We really don't know what the term "significant" actually means.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll let the witness -- if the witness wants to give an answer, Your Honour, I'll accept for these purposes his interpretation of what's "significant" as opposed to "insignificant" or "trivial."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please answer, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, leaving aside the documents, because to tell you the truth I didn't have any time to look at them, I've just received them. Let me first of all say this: We're talking about the time-period from the 19th until the 27th October, 1993, and I was saying that in Mostar the communication lines were down in mid-May 1992 and that from that time on we started with our effort to re-establish and repair the communications. So this is more than a year. We were not just sitting there idle. We were working, we were setting up communication lines. So at that time there were enough sufficient civilian lines in place and I assume also military lines. Secondly, let us look at document number 10315, if that's the number. I'm looking at the text in Croatian. It's a letter that is signed. This could have been sent by post, by courier, by helicopter, I don't know. So it doesn't follow -- well, of course it could have been faxed. I can't see the markings that are usual on fax transmissions, but we don't know what this is. It's a time-period that is substantially after the time-period when the telecommunications centre in Mostar was destroyed, and we did a lot of work to establish those communications. I don't know what was done at what point in time, but quite a lot of those lines were up. So you can't say that I said that lines were down in May 1992 and then say -- if you're talking about October 1993, Well, you said that the lines were down. That's really quite incomprehensible. I can't accept it, no matter who is trying to put it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Can I ask for one moment how the communication was actually affected?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we're going to have to have a break soon. Let's break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Court is back in session. According to our calculation, you have 22 minutes left, Mr. Scott. I thought you had less than that, but I was told 22 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just before we begin so I don't forget at the end of the day, please, we owe -- the Prosecution owes a response to the 1D objection -- I guess the Prlic Defence objections concerning Mr. Puljic, which I think is otherwise due today. I would be most grateful if the Chamber would allow us to file that tomorrow instead of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber grants you your motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, staying on the topic of Stupni Do, and again my purpose is not to go into the substance of what did or did not happen at Stupni Do but as a matter of -- related to the topic of communications, can I ask you to next look, please, at P 10620 in binder 2 of the general, so to speak, Prosecution binder, binder number 2, 10620. And, sir, while you're looking at that I'll say for the record this is a compilation of, I believe, nine media articles either from Bosnia-Herzegovina media or Croatian, Zagreb, media concerning the events that occurred in Stupni Do. The first is from Oslobodjenje, the 25th of October; the second one is from Vjesnik, which is a Zagreb newspaper; the third is from Slobodna Dalmacija, a Croatian newspaper, 27 October. And I'm not going to go through them all, but they are a series of news articles starting on the 25th of October and the last one being I believe the 31st -- yes, the 31st of October, again in Vjesnik titled: "Republic of Croatia condemns all crimes." And my point again, sir, in showing this to you is: Did you consider or would you consider in terms of the topic of communication that in Croatia at the time, in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, media and media reporting was another means of communication of information?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if we have the time again to go through all these articles, they -- you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that these all indicate -- these all involve reports or flows of information from somewhere, since some of these reporters are in Mostar, some of them are in other places, Zagreb, reference to Zagreb, HINA, the Croatian news agency, the Slobodna Dalmacija being published from Zagreb, that itself would represent a flow of information or a communication of information concerning the events in Stupni Do at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Journalists of newspaper publishing companies and the television and radio stations have their teams that follow the domestic and international media, and that is where they get their information from. That's how I understood it, or they have journalists at the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And following on the topic of media coverage, could I ask you next, please, to go to -- it should be close by, I hope, in the same binder, P 10627, P 10627. Sir, this appears to be a report dated the 27th of September, 1993, titled: "Information about the performance of work and tasks regarding the establishment and functioning of the Croatian Radio of Herceg-Bosna." Did you have any knowledge at the time that during 1993 at least efforts were being made by Herceg-Bosna to establish something called Croatian Radio of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to correct the Prosecutor in his version of the name of the name of this company, and in the upper right-hand corner we have the public company of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. This radio is not called Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm referring -- well --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, the translation was incorrect. I apologise. The translation's not correct. I'm going to repeat. In the upper left-hand corner there is the name of the radio, public company - radio of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, counsel. I accept that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, were you generally aware of this -- around this time when an effort was being made to establish a radio station or radio network of the sort that is described in this document?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can direct your attention in particular to item number 4 in the actual body of the report, item number 4, which does indicate, it appears, it says: "The radio's own professional organizational unit for the transmission equipment" et cetera "has been established ..." And continuing to the end of that number, paragraph 4: "... to the extent that it has achieved a stable signal, a wide aware of service, and corresponding technical stability of the system (consistent with the war-time conditions)." Can you confirm, sir, that as of mid-1993 that radio station or network was in fact up and running?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that the network was functioning and it is functioning still today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can ask you to go a little -- it's not a numbered paragraph, I don't believe, but if you go past number 6 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps in fairness it would be justified to point out the name of the radio station. Witness, could you read in this number 4 the name of that radio station.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name is Croatian Radio of Herceg-Bosna. It is a public company, radio of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and it was called Radio Herceg-Bosna or Croatian Radio Herceg-Bosna. But the official name is what is written at the beginning of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm a bit surprised. Why do you say that in this official document the name in number 4 is not the official name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to repeat. When you establish a public company it receives its official name and it is being registered under that name in the register of companies at the appropriate court. In practice you could use different abbreviations, or usually nobody talked about that whole story public company and so on and so forth, they would just shorten it in their own way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, I just wanted to immediately warn about a mistake in the translation I don't -- or in the transcript, I don't know where it is, page 43, line 8, the witness as recorded in the transcript said literally: [In English] "... that the network was functioning and it is functioning still today." [Interpretation] In the original Croatian I heard that the witness said that the measure -- the radio network mostly functioned and functions to this day. In the transcript the word "mostly" is not recorded and from what the witness -- and from that one can conclude that it functioned all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, did you add that it was working most of the time? Because Mr. Kovacic heard that, that it was working most of the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is what I said because for stations like this you would need electricity, an electricity supply, it was in the hills. Often they would be without power or there would be some kind of malfunction that needed to be repaired. It was hard to get parts, so it did not continuously function but it did mostly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we move on to another part of the document could we just go back for information's sake to the first page under the first full paragraph -- well, it would be the second paragraph of the document under the first heading. Since I'm always one for dates, sir, do you see in the second paragraph that this indicates that the broadcast of this radio began on the 14th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, if I can ask you, please, where we were a moment ago that -- if you can go beyond item 6 you will come to a point where there is a paragraph that starts as follows, and I'll just read slowly and hopefully you'll see it. "The total programme orientation, editorial policy, and programme scheme are defined by the basic documents of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, with an emphasis on presenting the survey of the activities of the official bodies," I won't list them all, "HVO Main Staff," et cetera. "Special attention is dedicated to the situation on the front lines, so that daily events are reported on in the audio reports from all theatres of operation - from Stolac to Brcko. One can state that the defence of the area of Herceg-Bosna is very much present in the programme of the Croatian Radio of Herceg-Bosna through the statements issued by the Main Staff (which have recently been very timely and up-to-date), and a large number of reports coming from the Radio's own sources, as well as through other sections and programme units." And would it surprise you at all that the radio station was being used for these purposes in receiving information from, among other sources, press statements, if you will, issued by the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not surprised. Why would I be surprised? This was of the highest interest to all the people who lived in that area which was caught up in the war. At that time we were following all the possible media. The only media that informed the public about the situation and the problems were the radio stations, so we listened to any radio station we could receive, and of course just like all media, all radio stations in the world, they were trying to report from the front. I don't see anything strange in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, sir.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many journalists were killed at the front in attempts to inform their listeners and their viewers about the situation at the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with you, sir. Can we look very quickly, please, at P 05551 for two brief points. This would be in the first -- I believe the first Prosecution binder, P 05551. Sir, this is a -- while you're looking at that, let me just introduce it for purposes of the record. This is the minutes -- or excuse me, I apologise, not the minutes. It's the call for a meeting, if you will, call to convene the 52nd Session of the Government of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna on 4 October, the English has been mistranslated, I apologise, it should be 4 October 1993, and stating an agenda. And just two quick items. On number 6 approval of the tariff of the PTT, that would be the body of which you were president of the managing board; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And would that be the type of business that would come before the government concerning the PTT during this period from time to time?
